author: Kodao Productions
title: Detained journalist Cumpio receives international award
content:
The International Women’s Media Foundation (IWMF) bestowed on journalist Frenchie Mae Cumpio the 2026 Wallis Annenberg Justice for Women Journalists Award in a ceremony in New York City on Tuesday.




IWMF said it honors Cumpio for reporting on social inequality in the Eastern Visayas region, including land rights abuses, the killings of farmers, disaster response, and the impacts of militarized conflict under government policies.




The prize was named after the prominent American philanthropist and heiress who championed various environmental and social advocacies such as the Liberty Canyon Wildlife Crossings LGBTQ+ and HIV/AIDS charities.




IWMF cited that as a student journalist at the University of the Philippines-Tacloban, Cumpio rose quickly within alternative media networks, becoming a leading voice in regional and grassroots reporting.




Charged with crimes widely regarded as fabricated, IWMF said Cumpio’s work – and her continued imprisonment – highlights the use of legal mechanisms, including anti-terror laws and red-tagging, to silence independent media in the Philippines.




The announcement of the 2026 Wallis Annenberg Justice for Women Journalists Award in New York City. (Photo by Vince Reasonda/Altermidya)

content:

The protesters said plummeting farm gate prices and continuously rising costs of agricultural inputs have forced many farmers in the upland region to refuse farming or selling their produce at bottom level prices.

title: The Philippines’ ‘solar surge’ leaves many Filipinos behind
content:
Amid increasing energy prices, Filipinos are turning to solar – but upfront costs mean it remains out of reach for those who most need savings




By 

Samantha Beltran / Dialogue Earth




ids Salvador Badilles, a doctor in Las Piñas, a city just south of the Philippines’ capital Manila, transitioned to solar power and electric vehicles to offset rising costs from the energy crisis. In June, her family installed a 12.6-kilowatt, 20-panel system, as well as a 12-kilowatt solar hybrid inverter and 32-kilowatt-hour batteries.




“We are saving so much already on gas and monthly electric consumption,” Badilles tells Dialogue Earth. Her family now saves PHP 20,000 (USD 315) each month for a system that cost them PHP 700,000 (around USD 11,000), she notes: “Even air conditioning [for the whole day] is not a problem anymore.”




Jovi Solomon, a café owner in Bataan province, installed a 40-kilowatt (KW) solar panel system to offset her business’s electricity costs, setting her back PHP 880,000. She says this allows her to save PHP 10,000 a month on her power bill.




Interest in solar power has surged as Filipinos grapple with skyrocketing electricity rates that have worsened since the Gulf conflict began in late February. However, the trend has also highlighted the stark gap between those who can afford solar options and those who are priced out.

title: Duterte must appear at every trial date, ICC orders
content:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) ordered former president Rodrigo Duterte’s regular appearance once formal trial starts on November 30.




While permitting his absence in Monday’s status conference in preparation for the trial, ICC Trial Chamber III presiding judge Joanna Korner told defense lawyers the accused must be present at every trial date once it begins at the end of the month.




“Once the actual trial starts, we will expect attendance on a daily basis,” the British magistrate told Duterte’s lead defense counsel Peter Haynes.




A group campaigning for the former strongman’s accountability for his war on drugs welcomed Korner’s order, saying they “eagerly await Duterte’s presence in trial.”




“The ICC today has reminded Duterte that he must attend trial. We eagerly await to see Duterte’s presence before the judges and answer for his indefensible crimes against the Filipino people,” Duterte Panagutin Network-Europe spokesperson Icai Enriquez said.




The group pointed out that the ICC earlier ruled that the alleged mastermind of the deaths of thousands is fit to stand trial after the defense has exhausted all excuses and attempts to evade or postpone proceedings.




Trial dates, sitting hours




In Monday’s status conference, the ICC affirmed that formal trial will begin on November 30. The Court has yet to formally issue a detailed schedule of trial dates

title: ‘Make autonomy genuine,’ group urges BARMM Government
content:
A consortium that observed the recent elections for the creation of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) urged its newly created parliament to make their hard-won self-government genuine.




Katungod Bangsamoro, a non-partisan and Commission on Elections-accredited observer last September 14 polls, also said the BARMM Parliament must address the historical injustices committed against the Bangsamoro, resist elite capture, and uphold their right to self-determination.




The group made the appeal as the BARMM Parliament convened for the first time on Friday, an event it described as “an important milestone in the long struggle of the Bangsamoro people for self-determination, justice, and genuine autonomy.”




“It opens a new chapter in the peace process and offers an opportunity to turn decades of struggle, sacrifices, and negotiations into meaningful democratic governance,” Katungod Bangsamoro co-convenor Atty. Carlos Isagani Zarate said.




Can it? Will it?

They tell their visitors about the two-day trek from their forest communities under direct sun and drenching rain last January. They say they have never walked as far before. The land that has nurtured them suddenly meant harm, as the strangers will kill them if they are not allowed to dig. Who among them knew that the land that bore them sweet potatoes and cassavas had so many metals they hardly heard of before?

title: Commercialization of Bilibid land would violate prisoners’ rights, KAPATID warns
content:
Political prisoners’ support group KAPATID asked the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) to protect the rights of persons deprived of liberty (PDL), warning of a Bureau of Corrections’ (BuCor) plan to close and commercialize the New Bilibid Prison (NBP) reservation by 2028.




The group said the plan may escalate into a “dual human rights and land displacement crisis” that would force prisoner transfers and residents’ evictions.




“We are deeply concerned that the impending closure threatens not only prisoners facing forced transfers but also long-time residents facing displacement. Residents have sent distress messages reporting as many as three eviction notices, with proceedings already underway,” KAPATID spokesperson Fides Lim said.




Lim demands a full disclosure of BuCor’s land-use plan on the 366.7-hectare public property as well as a congressional inquiry in PDL conditions at the country’s biggest jail facility.




At the CHR’s civil society consultation on the Human Rights Situationer on Persons Deprived of Liberty (PDLs) on Wednesday, KAPATID urged the CHR to press for a halt to transfers and evictions pending a human rights review.




Protect NBP lands




KAPATID’s also launched its “Protect NBP Lands” campaign, calling for transparency, accountability, and meaningful participation by affected communities and civil society in decisions on the reservation’s future

Africa said the president should take a deep look as to why the value of the Philippine peso has taken a dive never before seen in the country’s history.




Africa said Marcos should stop blaming geopolitical pressures alone, such as the war in the Middle East, why the peso is currently the worst performing currency in Southeast Asia.




In an interview with reporters on Wednesday, Marcos urged Filipinos not to panic as the country’s currency breached P64 per US dollar several times this week, assuring the public that his government has the tools and reserves to keep the economy afloat.




Marcos said that the Philippines’ foreign exchange reserves are healthy enough to defend the peso. The president blamed the currency slide and broader price pressures to supply-side factors, especially oil and energy, due to the ongoing war in the Middle East.




“Oil we can do nothing about. Food, we can,” he said, assuring that the administration is working on ways to bring down food prices and ease the burden on Filipino consumers.




Africa, however, said the president’s words are not having their intended effects as the Philippines labors under its steepest inflation rate this year at 7.2 per cent.

“It is important for the House to accept the correctness of the decision, rather than adopting Malacañang’s stance that the Court committed ‘judicial overreach,’” Tinio said.




Tinio added provisions that need correction pertain to unprogrammed appropriations, insertions for thousands of questionable infrastructure projects in the guise of institutional amendments, as wells as lump sum allocations such as the so-called local government support fund.

Libel and cyber libel are being weaponized to intimidate journalists and undermine press freedom.




Late last week, Pulong Duterte filed a criminal complaint for cyber libel naming several journalists among the respondents. He filed the criminal complaint in Davao City. A few days later, a Davao City court issued a warrant of arrest for cyber libel, and veteran journalist Philip Lustre was arrested.  These charges appear to be fabricated and intended to intimidate journalists.




Mr. Lustre’s case exemplifies a fabricated charge and should raise concerns about the actions of both the prosecutor’s office and the court.




Some argue that the Court is not at fault for issuing the warrant of arrest, as it is a procedural step, and is automatically issued, after the case is raffled. However, both the prosecutor’s office and the Court share responsibility.




It appears that Mr. Lustre was not given the opportunity to participate in the Preliminary Investigation. The investigating prosecutor proceeded without proof that Mr. Lustre was properly notified via subpoena. This raises concerns about whether respondents are properly served at their address. title: A hollow victory: On the SC decision declaring parts of the 2024-2026 budgets unconstitutional
content:
By 

Atty. Ephraim B. Cortez




In a recent decision, the Supreme Court declared the Unprogrammed Appropriation in the 2024, 2025, and 2026 General Appropriations Acts (GAA) unconstitutional. The Court found that Congress and the Bicameral Conference Committee committed grave abuse of discretion amounting to a lack or excess of jurisdiction for the following reasons:







The grant of authority to avail of the Unprogrammed Appropriation by the mere existence of any excess revenues from a specific source without considering the aggregate amount of revenue generated from all other sources is unconstitutional.







The pertinent provision of the GAA providing the condition for availment states:




“1. Availment of the Unprogrammed Appropriations. The amounts authorized herein for purpose Nos. 2-4,6, and 9-10 may be used when any of the following exists:




“a. Excess revenue collections in any of the identified non-tax revenue sources from its corresponding revenue collection target, as reflected in the Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing (BESF);




“b. New revenue collections or those arising from new tax or non-tax sources which are not part of, nor included in, the original revenue sources reflected in the BESF;




“c. Approved loans for foreign-assisted projects.




As written, any excess revenue triggers the availment of the Unprogrammed Appropriations.

title: Philippines now in worst hunger crisis in 3 decades
content:
More Filipinos are experiencing hunger and even more admitted to being poorer in the third quarter of the year, a national survey reveals. Nearly a quarter of Filipinos said they experienced “being hungry and having nothing to eat at least once in the past three months.”




In a study conducted from September 21 to 27, survey firm Social Weather Station (SWS) said that 22.6 per cent of respondent families admitted to experiencing involuntary hunger, up by 2.3 points from 20.3 per cent in June.




It was the worse hunger rate in the country since 1998. This year’s hunger incidence is worse by 1.5 points above the record-high 21.1 per cent average of 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic




Where in the Philippines is hunger worse?




Hunger is worse in the capital region of Metro Manila at 27 per cent, the survey said, followed by Mindanao at 23.7 per cent.




Poverty is as bad in the rest of Luzon at 23.6 per cent while the Visayas region has fallen to 16.0 per cent.




This translates to an estimated 16.8 million Filipino families considered themselves poor in September, up from 13.6 million in June.




The September 2026 survey also found that 55 per cent of Filipino families rated themselves as “poor” while 9 per cent rated themselves as “borderline poor”

title: Peso dives to new record low
content:
The Philippine Peso dove to a new record low on Thursday, breaching past the P63 threshold per US dollar for the first time in history. The Peso-Dollar exchange rate closed at P63.15 per US greenback. The previous record was P62.925 per US dollar set exactly a month ago on September 15.




The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) cited a stronger US dollar, shifting expectations around US Federal Reserve rate cuts, and regional market pressures brought about by the prolonged war in the Middle East as the reasons for the dive.




The Philippine currency had lost P5.21 to the US dollar since the US-Israel led war against Iran started in February 28.




The new record low happened as the BSP played conservative in defending the peso against the volatile foreign exchange market, choosing to preserve its reserves and intervening only when movements become sharp and disorderly.




The BSP primarily uses the country’s Gross International Reserves to stabilize the Philippine peso against foreign exchange volatility and to service foreign debt obligations.




The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), meanwhile, said electronic products and petroleum products, such as crude oil and refined fuel are two top importations that drain the country’s foreign exchange and import outlays.

TANZA, Cavite — At dawn, murmur start to break a market’s relative silence a moment back. As fisherfolk unload their catch and display them on the glistening floor wet with seawater, buyers lean in on their ears to whisper their bid on tubs brimming with fish. As more are unloaded and other bidders join in. The hum become din, waking a fish port from a trance as the sun rises.




Fish, crabs, shrimp, squid, shellfish and other marine products are sold and bought at Julungan Fish by whispering. The bidder who whispers the highest amount wins. Fishers and fishmongers call it 

bulungan

The bidding starts. (Photo by Jasmin Julia Rusios/Kodao)
